title: Grieving Together
author: Everett Henes
summary: Everett Henes, an Orthodox Presbyterian pastor and father of five, writes to husbands about how to love and shepherd their wives after miscarriage, beginning with his own family's loss during seminary and the years he secretly feared an argument had caused it. His central argument is that the husband's instinct to put his head down and turn the loss into tasks can leave his wife feeling she has lost both her child and her husband. Grounding his counsel in Ephesians 5 and 1 Peter 3:7, he defines the husband's role as attentive, sacrificial care whose first call is simply to remain near. The piece moves through a sequence of practical and theological disciplines: grieving together without insisting on identical grief, sharing sorrow without making the wife his caretaker, refusing false guilt and thin explanations about providence, and shepherding in ordinary ways such as handling appointments, meals, intrusive questions, difficult anniversaries and patience about intimacy. It closes with Christian hope for children who die in infancy, rooted in 2 Samuel 12, the Westminster Confession and the resurrection, and in the husband's role as an undershepherd who points his wife to Christ.
points: Henes warns that a husband who manages the crisis but never enters the grief risks leaving his wife feeling doubly bereaved.
He insists spouses grieve the same child differently, and neither should make his or her manner of grieving the standard for the other.
Husbands should refuse invented guilt and avoid platitudes like "everything happens for a reason," confessing only actual sin while admitting they do not know God's hidden purposes.
Shepherding is concrete: attending appointments, taking over household duties, controlling what is shared, remembering due dates and Mother's Day, and never pressing a timetable for intimacy.
He grounds hope not in infant innocence but in God's mercy in Christ, citing the Westminster Confession on elect infants and the resurrection.
quotes: This experience taught me that while miscarriage is common, it is never commonplace for the husband and wife who lose their child. Common does not mean “small.” A child was anticipated, loved, prayed for, and already given a place in the family’s future.

The danger is that he may turn the entire loss into a series of tasks. He manages the crisis but never enters the grief. He works longer hours, finds projects around the house, or occupies his mind with anything that keeps him from remembering. Meanwhile, his wife may feel that she has lost both her child and, for a time, her husband.
The husband cannot fix her grief. His first call is simpler and harder: to remain near her. He can say, “I am here. I miss our child too. You do not have to carry this alone.

Temperament matters. Some women process sorrow quietly, while some men need to speak. Some husbands feel the loss immediately; others begin to feel it weeks later. Neither spouse should make his or her manner of grieving the standard for the other.

Confession is appropriate where there has been actual sin. A husband who was harsh should confess his harshness. But neither spouse should transform ordinary failures into a secret explanation of God’s providence. We are responsible for the sins God reveals, not for causes we invent.

He should remember that physical recovery and grief do not follow the same timetable. The expected due date may be especially difficult. So may Mother’s Day, a later pregnancy announcement, or the birth of another child in the family or church. A wise husband remembers these moments and moves toward his wife before she must ask.

A grieving husband is not his wife’s savior. He cannot explain the providence, remove every fear, or call their child back from death. He is an undershepherd in the home, also in need of the Good Shepherd. Yet he can remain. He can listen. He can weep.
